question.knowledge_point: Rewriting One of the Limits of an Improper Integral
question.problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to 
${\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{\text{d}x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}?$
question.worked_solution:
This is an improper integral of the second kind because the function under the integral is unbounded as we approach the *lower* integration limit from any point that lies in the interval $x\in (1,4):$

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}\to \infty \,\text{as}\,x\to {1}^{+}
$$

We can attempt to evaluate this integral by integrating $f(x)$ over the interval $x\in [a,4]$ and taking the limit as $a\to {1}^{+}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to {1}^{+}}({\int }_{a}^{4}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x)\end{aligned}
$$
